comments.author: @pamlemm903
comments.text:
The alpha fold concept is actually much more complicated. We were not able to determine what is called the tertiary and quaternary structure of many proteins while being able to determine the primary structure, their sequence. We can use their sequence to recognize simple shapes like the alpha-helics and the beta-pleated sheets, and we call this level of structure secondary. But to compute all of the relevant dynmic values of a given seqience (and the temporal constraint/condition simulated by the building of the sequence one codon at a time (one set of three amino acids at a time) the introduction of each set fundamentally changes the conformation (according to the relevant thermodynamics) of the sequence thus accumulated. Meaning a protein with 100 codons goes through 100 stages of conformational change to arrive at its final conformation at the end of protein synthesis. That's tertiary structure. Even then, most proteins operate in complexes (multiple proteins thermodynamically bound to each other), which adds a whole new layer of complexity we refer to as quaternary structure. 

Without knowing anything about it, I'm guessing we fed alpha fold data that amounted to primary structure (sequence) and it manifested a neural-net based 'mind-image' of the tertiary structure of those sequences. Which is pretty remarkable to say the least! The computational power necessary to balance all the thermodynamic forces at play in protein folding is astronomical. But if you simply know all the associated values  then changing one value changes all the other values at the same time to result in a less computation-heavy analysis. (like pulling one node in a net, you can tell, to a certain degree, how all the other nodes will move in relation to each other and that imposed pull). It's a pattern of relationship, not a brute force calculation of all values. Being that we cannot comprehend such complex/complicated things, especially when they are not open to observation with the naked eye or consistent with newtonian physics, we see it's ability to comprehend that pattern as astonishing.

comments.author: @matteyas
comments.text:
the reason some are "certain" is because of two things.
1) we don't know the space of possible intelligences, but it's quite likely that it's huge
2) we don't know the space of behavior that a specific intelligence will engage in, but it's easier to do bad stuff than good stuff (aligning with our preferences is difficult; even just to describe what that means with good enough detail is beyond us)

if those two things are true, and people are just rolling the dice, summoning random intelligences out of this space… what are the chances we'll pull out the benevolent god we want? how many demons are in there? so there is a convergence here, where the specification (those two things i just mentioned) together with there being uncertainty, is all we need to know to say that this is almost certainly disastrous.

it's like taking a map of a minefield where the amount and placement of mines is unknown, having a monkey draw a bunch of lines on it, let someone pick a path that "looks safe" (this is how we summon "safe" models currently), and then following that path. sure, there's lots of uncertainty, but i can tell you that it's a bad idea for sure, and it will almost certainly end in disaster.

of course, if the map is like 1000m² and there's just one mine, it'd be a different matter. the problem here is that nobody has been able to put any numbers at all on this particular map, or even make a single credible argument that the number of mines is small. maybe there are zero mines! but maybe there's almost only mines, like any other difficult project. until someone can tell me numbers, and reasons for those numbers, i'm going to just go out on a limb and say that (1) and (2) above are very reasonable, and as such, some sort of doom is reasonably certain.

still, maybe i've missed something. maybe something else, that just happens to be benign, is even more convergent. waiting for the good arguments, and also leaving a reasonably big slice of probability unchecked. say, 10% likelihood that things will "happily just go well for some reason!" currently, most of that slice consists of things like "maybe we actually will hit a wall" or "maybe intelligence has compassion or curiosity or similar as inevitable convergences." (it's easy to say that any increasingly intelligent agent will at some point have access to compassion—or any other property—it's almost inevitable since having the option is always more optimal. what's difficult to know is how often compassion will be used over other priorities. our species has examples of all manner of events; some where compassion is overflowing, and some where compassion is completely devoid. again, uncertainty here is enough to warrant near certainty in bad outcomes.)

The "car safety" analogy is way off. A closer analogy is a new type of rocket ship, where we're looking to put ALL of humanity on board.

1. Think vehicles are safe by default, and rockets will be no different.

--

Camps 1, 2 and 3 need more evidence to back their claims, but the precautionary principal makes sense until we have more evidence. And to be fair, more and more evidence keeps stacking for camps 3 and 4.
